name: Hudson v. McMillian
event: Review follows reversal of an $800 damages award entered after a consensual trial before a magistrate.
questions: Whether the Fifth Circuit applied the correct Eighth Amendment test when it rejected the claim arising from this incident of force for lack of significant injury. The accepted question does not require a general definition of punishment for every unauthorized assault.
baseline: The three February 25 decisions are uncoordinated and share the law effective through January 27; none uses another February 25 decision as entering law.
record: Hudson seeks removal of the significant-injury bar; respondents seek affirmance, including on an asserted isolated/unauthorized-conduct ground. The October 30, 1983 beating occurred while Hudson was handcuffed and shackled. Undisturbed findings establish unnecessary blows by McMillian and Woods and express supervisory condonation by Mezo. Bruising, facial swelling, loosened teeth and a cracked dental plate accompanied the blows. The court of appeals found the force clearly excessive and wanton but treated the injuries as minor. No new injury, motive or damages finding is made.
entering: The October 7 Holdings and Standards and Tests are empty opening registers. Whitley v. Albers, 475 U.S. 312, governs malicious-and-sadistic force during a prison disturbance; Estelle v. Gamble, 429 U.S. 97, requires deliberate indifference to serious medical needs; Wilson v. Seiter, 501 U.S. 294, separates objective deprivation and subjective culpability in confinement conditions. These different constitutional settings do not yet yield a controlling universal force rule in this term. Hafer (simulated November 5) preserves personal-capacity actions and distinct defenses. Hunter (simulated December 16) applies reasonable-officer immunity on the supported Rule 56 record. Neither changes the presented injury element. Ordinary civil proof and clear-error review of trial facts remain; the additional legal element receives independent review.
reach: Section 1983 supplies the action for the convicted prisoner’s Eighth Amendment claim. The trial findings are not displaced. The grant limitation recorded at 500 U.S. 903 is respected. Immunity, psychological injury alone, increased compensation and prison-management relief are not reached.
stoneCheck: The entering law and corrected argument date do not displace any fixed choice. Stone votes to reverse and remand; he joins Parts A and C at the scope stated below, which reproduce his approved injury rule, record application and express reservation. He does not join the proposed universal mental-state rule in Part B. No assumption about immunity at the 1983 incident is attributed to him.
action: The Fifth Circuit is reversed, 7–2, and the case is remanded for further disposition consistent with the undisturbed trial findings and the rejection of the significant-injury bar.

components.title: Significant-injury dismissal
components.remedy: Further disposition consistent with undisturbed findings; no increase in the $800 award, new immunity ruling or injunction.

holdings.title: Limited injury does not defeat this established nontrivial malicious beating
holdings.rule: A nontrivial beating inflicted maliciously and without disciplinary justification on a restrained convicted prisoner violates the Eighth Amendment even when the resulting physical injuries are limited, where the established conduct satisfies even Whitley’s demanding malicious-and-sadistic inquiry. Injury remains relevant evidence and bears on compensation; accidental harm or a merely technical battery is not enough.
holdings.authority: Part A of O’Connor’s opinion, joined by Stone, White, Stevens, Kennedy and Souter: six Justices adopt this rule and its application. The general extension proposed in Part B has only four votes.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that the Constitution does not make protection from this beating depend on how much lasting injury the prisoner suffered. Whitley v. Albers distinguishes a good-faith effort to preserve discipline from force maliciously and sadistically applied to cause harm; the findings here satisfy even that demanding inquiry. Hudson was restrained, no force was needed, the guards repeatedly struck him, and their supervisor condoned the assault. His dental and facial injuries also establish that the force was not trivial. Wilson v. Seiter requires an objective constitutional deprivation, but its treatment of confinement conditions does not impose a separate significant-medical-injury requirement on these established acts of violence. Estelle v. Gamble supplies the prohibition on unnecessary and wanton pain while retaining its distinct medical-care requirements. The contrary injury floor would excuse serious custodial violence because the victim happened to withstand it. The Court leaves a comprehensive mental-state rule for other force settings, psychological injury alone, individual defenses and lawful measurement of damages undecided.
precedents: *Whitley v. Albers*, 475 U.S. 312 — applied as a sufficient ground on these findings; its disturbance rule remains in force, but a universal extension receives no majority here.

*Wilson v. Seiter*, 501 U.S. 294 — distinguished by the character of the constitutional wrong; the objective-deprivation requirement survives without becoming a significant-injury floor for this beating.
*Estelle v. Gamble*, 429 U.S. 97 — applied for unnecessary and wanton pain; serious medical need and deliberate indifference remain the medical-care rules.

nonholding: Part C rejects the alternate characterization on this record: the undisturbed supervisory-condonation finding and the granted question prevent affirmance on an assumed isolated, unauthorized assault. It announces no general rule defining punishment. Part B’s proposed universal Whitley standard is a four-Justice position. No Marks aggregation supplies a universal mental-state rule: the six-Justice narrow holding already controls this case, and the other writings do not adopt a common broader rationale. The ordinary exclusion of trivial force is not converted into an exhaustive rule for all unusual forms of cruelty.
law: Effective February 25, 1992, significant injury is not an additional necessary element for the established nontrivial malicious custodial beating described in Part A. Before this decision, Whitley directly governed disturbance-related force and Wilson governed conditions; afterward, the six-Justice application resolves this nontrivial beating without adopting a universal mental-state standard. The existing rules for medical care, conditions, legitimate discipline, personal defenses and compensatory proof remain distinct. No new mandatory test for every prison-force setting is created.
separate: O’Connor, joined by White, Kennedy and Souter in Part B, would apply Whitley’s malicious-and-sadistic standard to all prison force claims. That formulation has four votes. Stevens would reserve that heightened formulation for serious disturbances and otherwise apply the unnecessary-and-wanton-pain inquiry, although he agrees the heightened standard is met here. Blackmun likewise rejects a universal extension and rejects an injury floor that would shield intentional cruelty. Thomas, joined by Scalia, would require a serious objective deprivation as well as culpable intent; his view does not require permanent or visible physical injury in every case.
continuity: O’Connor/White/Kennedy/Souter, Part B, February 25: universal Whitley force standard; four-Justice noncontrolling proposition. Stevens, concurrence, same date: unnecessary-and-wanton pain suffices outside serious disturbances; higher standard met here. Blackmun, judgment concurrence, same date: opposes universal Whitley extension; constitutional pain may include substantial psychological harm, and docket reduction cannot define a substantive constitutional right. That psychological issue is unpresented and noncontrolling. Thomas/Scalia, dissent, same date: serious objective deprivation required, potentially nonphysical; State remedies and their constitutional adequacy remain a distinct route. No later treatment yet.
procedure: Supreme Court merits review ends with reversal and remand. The Fifth Circuit must dispose of the case consistently with the intact findings and without its significant-injury bar. No amount above the existing $800 award is ordered; no immunity defense or broader injunction is adjudicated. No Supreme Court implementation jurisdiction is retained.
dependencies: Later force cases must distinguish the narrow six-Justice holding from the four-Justice universal standard. Collins and McCarthy may use only the former, without replacing their distinct due-process and medical-care elements.
formBasis: the controlling scope and coalition differ: the universal Whitley extension lacks a majority, and the remand is expressly confined to the approved record; partial joins require separate judgment and topology tables.

alternatives: The serious-injury path relies on Wilson’s objective requirement and the need to distinguish constitutional wrongs from ordinary battery. The opposing path locates objective gravity in this nontrivial malicious violence, with Whitley supplying a sufficient culpability showing and injury remaining probative. The latter has a majority. The broader universal culpability path loses its fifth vote when the approved limited position is assembled; White/O’Connor/Kennedy/Souter retain it, while Stevens and Blackmun retain their objections. No vote is shifted to manufacture a majority. The isolated-assault alternative cannot rest on facts contrary to the intact findings or exceed the grant.
auditFinal: Final arithmetic: reversal/remand 7–2; narrow Part A and scope Part C each six; universal Part B four. Blackmun’s judgment vote is not counted as a join. Stone’s partial joins track his expressly approved propositions; no universal force rule or new trivial-force exception is attributed to him. No independently sufficient alternative merits holding is omitted. Fresh-audit caution incorporated: the rule expressly states satisfaction of Whitley’s malicious-and-sadistic inquiry as sufficient here. No material non-Stone commitment change or new historical departure requires a second reconciliation.
